name: Half Guard Pass
description: Master Half Guard Pass in BJJ. Strategic guide covering passing mechanics, pressure systems, and control transitions from both top and bottom perspectives.
variant_uniqueness: Transitional passing phase with leg trapped
overview:
Half Guard Pass represents the critical transitional battleground where the top player works to overcome the bottom player's leg entanglement while the bottom player fights to retain guard or sweep. This position exists in the dynamic tension between established half guard control and complete pass completion to side control or mount. Understanding both perspectives—the systematic pressure and leg extraction from top, and the retention frames and sweep threats from bottom—is essential for mastering this fundamental BJJ position.

From a strategic perspective, half guard passing has evolved into one of the most technical areas of modern BJJ. The position requires the top player to systematically dismantle defensive structures (knee shield, underhook, lockdown) while maintaining forward pressure and base. The bottom player must create frames, establish underhooks, and threaten sweeps to prevent the pass. The battle for underhook control, crossface dominance, and leg positioning determines the outcome more than raw strength or athleticism.

The half guard pass position serves as a gateway to dominant positions and submission opportunities. Top players who master pressure distribution, timing, and systematic passing sequences can achieve high-percentage pass completion rates. Bottom players who understand retention mechanics, sweep timing, and recovery pathways can neutralize even skilled passers. This position exemplifies the chess-like nature of BJJ, where positional understanding and technical precision overcome size and strength advantages.
key_principles: Control hierarchy: Upper body control must be established before attempting leg extraction
Pressure distribution: Chest and shoulder pressure creates cumulative fatigue in bottom player
Underhook battle: Controlling inside space determines offensive and defensive opportunities
Systematic dismantling: Remove defensive structures sequentially rather than forcing pass
Base management: Free leg positioning provides stability while enabling directional changes
Timing and patience: Rushing creates sweep opportunities; methodical pressure creates openings
Dilemma creation: Threaten submissions to accelerate passing or force defensive reactions

bottom.overview:
Half Guard Pass Bottom Position represents the defensive perspective where you maintain leg entanglement on one of the top player's legs while working to prevent pass completion, threaten sweeps, or recover to better guard positions. This position requires active defensive framing, underhook battles, and constant adjustment to the top player's passing attempts. Success depends on maintaining connection while creating angles and opportunities for sweeps or guard recovery.

From the bottom perspective, half guard retention is not passive defense but an active battle for positional control. You must establish frames to prevent crushing pressure, fight for underhooks to enable offensive opportunities, and use leg configurations (knee shield, lockdown, deep half) to neutralize passing attempts. The key principle is creating layers of defense that force the top player to solve multiple problems simultaneously, buying time for sweeps or recovery.

Modern half guard bottom game has evolved to include sophisticated retention systems, sweep chains, and submission threats that make this position highly effective even against skilled passers. Understanding when to maintain retention versus when to transition to deep half, lockdown, or other guard recovery positions is essential for developing a complete half guard bottom game.
state_invariants: One of top player's legs remains trapped between your legs in half guard configuration, with your inside leg controlling their knee line and outside leg hooking around their trapped leg
You maintain at least one defensive frame (knee shield, hand frames, or underhook) to prevent top player from achieving crushing chest pressure and complete flattening
Your body positioning allows hip mobility for shrimping, angle creation, or transitional movements to sweeps or guard recovery positions

Threaten sweeps to force top player into defensive reactions

common_errors.error: Remaining flat on back and accepting top player's chest pressure
common_errors.consequence: Loses ability to create frames, becomes immobilized, and pass becomes inevitable
common_errors.correction: Stay on side, create space with frames, maintain hip mobility through constant micro-adjustments

common_errors.error: Failing to fight for underhook when opportunity presents
common_errors.consequence: Top player establishes crossface control, eliminates offensive options, and controls passing angles
common_errors.correction: Aggressively pursue underhook on trapped leg side, use it immediately for sweeps or to prevent crossface

common_errors.error: Static knee shield without active pressure or adjustment
common_errors.consequence: Top player smashes through shield or goes around it, achieving pass position
common_errors.correction: Keep knee shield active with constant pressure into opponent's chest, adjust angle based on their movements

common_errors.error: Gripping without purpose or holding static grips too long
common_errors.consequence: Arms become fatigued, grips get broken, and defensive structure collapses
common_errors.correction: Use grips actively to control distance and angles, release and re-grip as needed to conserve energy

common_errors.error: Allowing top player to consolidate position without resistance
common_errors.consequence: Top player establishes headquarters or heavy control making retention nearly impossible
common_errors.correction: Constant movement and adjustment, never allow top player to settle into comfortable position

common_errors.error: Neglecting lockdown or deep half entries when heavily pressured
common_errors.consequence: Accepts disadvantageous position without exploring alternative defensive structures
common_errors.correction: Transition to lockdown or deep half when pressure becomes too heavy to maintain standard half guard

common_errors.error: Overcommitting to single sweep attempt without backup options
common_errors.consequence: Top player defends and uses your commitment against you to complete pass
common_errors.correction: Chain sweeps together, use initial attempt to create reactions that open other opportunities

training_drills.name: Half Guard Retention Against Progressive Pressure
training_drills.description: Partner applies increasing pressure from half guard top while you work to maintain frames, underhook battles, and positional integrity. Start at 30% pressure and increase to 70% over multiple rounds. Focus on staying on side, maintaining frames, and creating movement.

training_drills.name: Underhook Battle Drill
training_drills.description: Start in neutral half guard position. Both players fight for underhook control. Bottom player works to establish and maintain underhook while top player works to prevent and remove it. Reset when underhook is clearly established or completely denied.

training_drills.name: Sweep Chain Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Practice flowing between different half guard sweeps (underhook sweep, old school, deep half entries) based on partner's defensive reactions. Partner provides progressive resistance and presents different defensive structures. Emphasize smooth transitions and recognizing sweep opportunities.

training_drills.name: Positional Sparring from Half Guard Bottom
training_drills.description: Start in half guard bottom position and work exclusively for sweeps or guard retention while partner works for passes. Reset to half guard bottom after successful sweep or completed pass. Track success rates and identify problem areas.

expert_insights.danaher: From the bottom perspective of half guard pass defense, the fundamental principle is creating layers of defensive structure that force the top player to solve multiple problems sequentially. The common error is accepting a single defensive layer—such as just maintaining the leg entanglement without frames or underhook battles. The sophisticated approach recognizes that half guard retention requires simultaneous management of multiple defensive elements: leg configuration (standard, knee shield, lockdown), upper body frames, underhook control, and hip mobility. The biomechanical reality is that if the top player achieves crossface control while you're flat on your back, retention becomes exponentially more difficult. Therefore, the primary technical imperative is preventing flattening by staying on your side, maintaining active frames, and creating constant angular adjustments. The underhook battle is particularly critical because it determines whether you have offensive options or are purely defensive. When you establish the underhook on the trapped leg side, you immediately gain access to sweeping mechanics and can prevent the crossface that otherwise dominates your upper body. The systematic approach to half guard bottom is recognizing when standard retention is becoming untenable and transitioning to alternative structures like deep half or lockdown before the top player consolidates crushing control.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, half guard bottom is one of my go-to positions for tiring out aggressive passers and setting up sweeps. The key insight from high-level matches is that you can't be static in half guard bottom—you have to be constantly creating problems for the passer. My approach is to immediately establish knee shield and fight for the underhook because these two elements give me both defensive security and offensive potential. When the top player commits heavy pressure to smash my knee shield, that's when I transition to deep half or lockdown. If they try to back step or go around, I'm ready with old school sweeps or guard recovery. The mental game is critical here too—a lot of guys panic when they feel heavy pressure and try to explode out, which usually results in getting passed. Instead, I stay calm, maintain my frames, and wait for them to make a mistake or create an opening. In my experience, even the best passers will eventually give you something if you're patient and technical. The competition-proven approach is having a hierarchy of defenses: knee shield as first line, underhook battles as second line, and transitions to deep half or lockdown as third line when pressure becomes too heavy. This systematic defense has allowed me to retain guard against elite passers and tire them out in the process.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The 10th Planet approach to half guard bottom is all about creating offensive opportunities from what looks like a defensive position. We developed the lockdown specifically to give bottom players more control and sweep options when top players are trying to pass. When you're in half guard bottom and feeling pressure, the lockdown gives you the ability to break down their posture, control their base, and set up sweeps like the electric chair or old school. The key innovation is recognizing that half guard bottom doesn't have to be a desperate scramble—it can be a strategic position where you're actually controlling the pace. The knee shield is crucial for keeping space and preventing smash passes, but you need to be ready to transition. If they commit too much pressure to smash your shield, go to deep half. If they try to backstep, you've got old school or underhook sweeps. The creative element is using the lockdown to create moments where you're actually controlling them even though they're on top. Breaking their posture with the lockdown, lifting with your hips, and creating that moment of off-balance is when sweeps become high-percentage. In no-gi especially, the lockdown becomes even more important because there are no gi grips to rely on for control. The 10th Planet methodology teaches that half guard bottom is one of the best positions to learn because it teaches you to be comfortable being uncomfortable and to create offense from defense.

top.overview:
Half Guard Pass Top Position represents the offensive perspective where you are actively working to overcome the bottom player's half guard retention while maintaining dominant positioning and control. One of your legs is trapped between the bottom player's legs, but you have established positional advantages (underhooks, crossface, pressure) and are positioned to complete the pass to side control, mount, or other dominant positions. This position requires systematic pressure application, proper weight distribution, and the ability to neutralize defensive structures while extracting your trapped leg.

From the top perspective, half guard passing is a methodical process of dismantling defensive layers rather than explosive advancement. You must establish upper body control first (crossface or underhook), then systematically remove the bottom player's defensive structures (knee shield, frames, underhooks), and finally extract your trapped leg while maintaining control. The key principle is creating immobility in the bottom player's hips and shoulders before attempting the final pass.

Modern half guard passing has evolved toward smash-passing techniques, headquarters positioning, and systematic leg extraction methods that neutralize retention while creating submission opportunities. Understanding when to apply crushing pressure versus when to use mobility and tactical passing is essential for developing a complete half guard passing game that works against all levels of opposition.

common_errors.error: Bringing weight too far back or sitting upright

common_errors.consequence: Bottom player maintains mobility to turn into you, establish frames, create recovery angles, or threaten sweeps

common_errors.error: Poor base with free leg allowing it to be too close or too extended

common_errors.error: Rushing the pass without addressing defensive layers systematically
common_errors.consequence: Bottom player maintains retention mechanisms, pass is blocked or reversed
common_errors.correction: Follow systematic sequence: establish crossface, prevent underhook, clear knee shield or frames, control hips, then extract leg and complete pass

common_errors.error: Allowing bottom player to turn to their side and establish strong frames
common_errors.consequence: Creates defensive structure that is difficult to pass, enables guard recovery and sweep opportunities
common_errors.correction: Keep bottom player's shoulders flat to mat with chest pressure, attack underhook side proactively, use weight distribution to prevent turning

common_errors.error: Gripping without purpose or maintaining static grips
common_errors.consequence: Energy waste, telegraphs intentions, allows bottom player to counter-grip effectively
common_errors.correction: Use grips actively to control specific threats, break grips that give bottom player advantages, transition grips as you progress through passing sequence

expert_insights.danaher: The half guard pass represents one of the most technically demanding positions in ground fighting because it requires simultaneous management of multiple defensive systems while maintaining offensive pressure. The fundamental mechanical problem is that you must extract your trapped leg while preventing the bottom player from using that same leg as a lever for sweeps or guard recovery. The solution lies in understanding that passing half guard is not a single technique but a systematic progression through defensive layers. First, you must establish head control or a crossface to limit the bottom player's mobility and prevent them from turning into you effectively. Second, you must control the inside space by preventing the underhook, as this is the bottom player's primary offensive weapon from half guard. Third, you must address their leg configuration, whether it's a knee shield, lockdown, or standard half guard structure. Only after systematically dismantling these defensive layers can you safely extract your leg and complete the pass. The practitioners who excel at passing half guard understand that pressure is not merely about weight distribution but about creating a constant forward vector that denies the bottom player the ability to create recovery angles. Your hips must perpetually drive toward their head while your upper body controls their ability to turn or frame effectively.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: Half guard passing is where matches are won or lost at the highest levels because everyone has a half guard game now. The key insight from competition is that you can't just power through good half guard retention, you need to create dilemmas. When I'm passing half guard, I'm immediately looking for the kimura grip on their underhook attempt because that's what everyone wants. Once they commit to that underhook, their arm is exposed and now they have to choose between defending the kimura or defending the pass, and usually they can't do both effectively. The crossface is absolutely critical, but it's not just about pushing their head away. You want to use the crossface to control their entire upper body rotation and create angles where they can't effectively use their frames. In competition, I've found that the knee slice is the highest percentage finish from half guard pass, but you have to set it up by first threatening other passes or submissions. If they're worried about a kimura or a darce setup, the knee slice becomes much easier because their defensive attention is divided. The other critical detail is pace. You can't give them time to establish their full defensive structure. You need to be constantly progressing, constantly attacking, forcing them to defend multiple threats simultaneously until something breaks down.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Half guard passing is all about understanding the game they're trying to play from bottom and shutting it down before it starts. From the 10th Planet perspective, we see so many different half guard variations—lockdown, electric chair setups, old school sweeps, deep half entries—and the key is recognizing what system they're trying to implement and attacking it early. When someone's playing lockdown, they want you to stay heavy and static so they can break you down and create sweep angles. The counter is to stay mobile, keep your weight shifting, and attack their lockdown with specific breaks while threatening submissions that make them choose between the sweep and defending their neck or arm. The crossface is crucial, but I also love the gift wrap from half guard pass when they're fighting for that underhook. You can wrap their arm up and take away their primary offensive tool while setting up devastating back takes or submissions. The other thing about half guard passing is that you should never be just passing—you should be threatening. Every passing attempt should have a submission component to it. Are you threatening a darce? A kimura? An arm crush? When you make passing and submission one combined attack, their defense becomes much more difficult because they can't focus entirely on retention. The modern game requires you to be fluid between passing systems. If the knee slice isn't there, can you transition to a long step? Can you go to a smash pass? That versatility and creativity in your passing game is what makes you unpredictable and ultimately successful.
